title: Low Expectations for Israel’s Election
gist: Only a teaser is available: Ben-Ami argues Netanyahu has overextended Israel's strategic commitments beyond its productive base while eroding allied goodwill, and that the Oct 27 election can at best install a law-abiding government, not a radically new foreign policy.

insights.claim: Israel's ever-increasing strategic commitments are outstripping the productive base that finances them under Netanyahu.
insights.speaker: SHLOMO BEN-AMI
insights.so_what: Watch Israeli fiscal and defense-financing strain as a structural risk factor.

insights.claim: Netanyahu's policies are destroying the goodwill on which Israel's alliances depend.
insights.speaker: SHLOMO BEN-AMI
insights.so_what: Erosion of allied support is a tail risk for Israeli security and financing.

insights.claim: A new Israeli government after the October 27 election would not transform foreign policy, though it could begin to pull Israel out of its morass.
insights.speaker: SHLOMO BEN-AMI
insights.so_what: Do not price a sharp foreign-policy pivot from a change of government.
insights.quote: A radically new foreign policy will remain out of reach.

insights.claim: Hungary's April election, where Orban's populist government lost to a center-right anti-corruption party, is offered as the best-case template for Israel.
insights.speaker: SHLOMO BEN-AMI
insights.so_what: Template for a non-radical, rule-of-law political turnover.
